title: Tesla owners to get insurance discount if they use self-drive tech
full_text:
Insurance giant Zurich says Australian customers will be able to access cheaper premiums if their Tesla is equipped with self-driving technology, a national first for the sector, despite lingering safety concerns around use of the software.
From Monday, the Swiss group will begin offering a risk-based reduction on insurance policies for Tesla electric vehicles that include its advanced driver-assist system that allows cars to navigate themselves on set routes with driver supervision – only the second market to do so globally.
“This expanded proposition offers the same high-quality insurance at a more affordable cost due to the reduced risk associated with supervised self-driving,” said Alex Morgan, Zurich’s head of general insurance.
Tesla, which makes Australia’s most popular EV, says it has collected over 132 million kilometres of local self-driving data and claims that a car fitted with the technology has one-seventh as many collisions.
Zurich didn’t provide a figure on how much drivers could save on their insurance with the technology, with the exact price to be determined alongside other risk factors such as age, location and driving record.
The offer will be included under Zurich’s existing InsureMyTesla package, which also offers excess-free windscreen replacement and covers damage to charging cables.
Tesla’s technology uses the car’s eight external cameras to capture 360-degree road vision, which is then fed into an artificial intelligence-powered neural network that makes decisions about accelerating, braking, indicating and lane changing. An internal camera focused on the driver, meanwhile, ensures they remain attentive and ready to take over. Twitter link
After launching in September last year, Australia became one of only 12 countries globally where Full Self-Driving (FSD) is available. It is offered as a monthly subscription for $149 per month and is equipped to cars via an over-the-air software download. About 50 cent of Tesla drivers purchase the technology.
“Full Self-Driving (Supervised) is making driving significantly safer and it’s encouraging to see InsureMyTesla by Zurich pioneering this benefit and reflecting the reduced risk for Tesla owners,” said Tesla’s country director Thom Drew.
The Tesla Model Y has been Australia’s most popular EV for more than three years and benefited from a renewed surge in demand this year as the conflict in the Middle East sent petrol prices soaring.
In May, the Model Y became the first EV to top national sales charts, a feat it backed up in June and August. It comes as chief executive Elon Musk rolled out Tesla’s driverless rideshare service in Texas this month.
Morgan said drivers would not have to prove that FSD was on during a collision, just that it was equipped to the car, and that the company would never receive any individual driver or vehicle data from Tesla, including whether FSD was active during an incident.
“The driver must always supervise and remain in control, and our policy is designed for people using driver-assistance technology in line with Australian law,” he said.
But Angus McKerral, a road safety researcher at the University of Melbourne, said he was concerned the technology, which remains imperfect, could make drivers dependent on it and less competent on the road.
FSD has been linked to several collisions in the US, including at least two fatal ones. University of Queensland researchers, meanwhile, said they recorded more than 500 safety incidents that required driver intervention across 100 days of local testing.
“My concern would be that reduced premiums are proposed based on a hypothetical ideal relationship between the driver monitoring for FSD failures, when in reality, drivers tend to blindly trust the system, leading to dangerous mistakes and simply substituting one risk for another,” McKerral said.
